content: Previous systematic reviews have not demonstrated a clear benefit of using glucocorticoids for treating acute viral bronchiolitis in infants and young children. Despite this, their use remains widespread. Recent large-scale clinical trials have contributed significantly to the existing body of evidence and have proposed new treatment strategies that include glucocorticoids. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of both systemic and inhaled glucocorticoids in children diagnosed with acute viral bronchiolitis. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared short-term systemic or inhaled glucocorticoids with either a placebo or another intervention. The study population included children under 24 months of age experiencing their first episode of bronchiolitis accompanied by wheezing. The primary outcomes assessed were hospital admissions by days 1 and 7 for outpatient settings and the length of hospital stay (LOS) for inpatient settings. Secondary outcomes included clinical severity, healthcare utilization, pulmonary function, symptom resolution, quality of life, and adverse effects. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, Scopus®, and IRAN MedEx, covering studies published up to January 2013. Two independent reviewers extracted data on study characteristics, participant demographics, interventions, and outcomes. The risk of bias was assessed, and the strength of evidence was graded. Meta-analyses were performed separately for inpatient and outpatient results using random-effects models. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were conducted, including those involving the combined use of bronchodilators as part of the treatment protocol. A total of 17 trials involving 2,596 participants were included in the review. Of these, three trials were determined to have a low overall risk of bias. The included studies exhibited significant heterogeneity in terms of baseline disease severity, glucocorticoid regimens, comparator interventions, and reported outcomes. The pooled analysis revealed that glucocorticoids did not significantly reduce outpatient admissions by day 1 (risk ratio [RR] 0.92; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.78 to 1.08) or day 7 (RR 0.86; 95% CI 0.70 to 1.06) when compared to placebo. Similarly, there was no significant reduction in the length of hospital stay for inpatients (mean difference -0.18 days; 95% CI -0.39 to 0.04). However, unadjusted results from a large factorial RCT with a low risk of bias indicated that a combination of high-dose systemic dexamethasone and inhaled epinephrine reduced outpatient admissions by day 7 (baseline admission risk of 26%; RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.44 to 0.95). The number needed to treat (NNT) was 11 (95% CI 7 to 76). Importantly, no significant differences in short-term adverse effects were observed with this combined therapy. No other comparisons demonstrated clinically meaningful differences in the primary outcomes. In conclusion, the current evidence does not support a clinically significant effect of systemic or inhaled glucocorticoids on reducing hospital admissions or the length of hospital stay in children with acute viral bronchiolitis. While the combination of dexamethasone and epinephrine may reduce outpatient admissions, these findings are exploratory, and the available safety data are limited. Further research is needed to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and broader applicability of this combined treatment approach.
